front: A bar magnet's north pole approaches a wire loop. What does the induced current do?
why: Lenz law applied to an approaching magnet is a standard induction question

front: A charge moving perpendicular to a uniform field travels in a circle of radius $r = {{c1::mv/(qB)}}$.
why: r = mv/(qB) is the core equation for charges in B fields and mass spec

front: A charged particle enters a field at an angle between $0$ and $90$ degrees. What path does it follow?
why: Helical path is a secondary case beyond the perpendicular circle

front: A conducting loop is pulled out of a field region. Which way does the induced current flow, and does pulling require work?
why: Work required to pull a loop out is second-step Lenz reasoning

front: A copper ring rests on the core of an electromagnet and the current is switched on. What happens to the ring?
why: Jumping-ring demo is an application of Lenz, plausible passage context

front: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force. The direction of this force is determined by:
why: F = ILB and the right-hand rule for wires are core outline content

front: A doubly charged ion follows a radius {{c1::half}} that of a singly charged ion of the same mass and speed.
why: Radius inversely proportional to charge is a common mass-spec discrete

front: A magnetic field cannot change a particle's:
why: Magnetic force never changes kinetic energy: tested nearly every year

front: A molecule such as $O_2$ with unpaired electrons is {{c1::paramagnetic}} and is drawn into a magnetic field.
why: O2 paramagnetism from unpaired electrons is a frequent discrete

why: Motor-vs-no-work paradox is conceptual depth beyond typical questions

front: A proton moves east through a magnetic field pointing north. Which way is the magnetic force?
why: Right-hand-rule direction on a moving proton is a perennial discrete

front: A proton moves exactly parallel to a magnetic field. What magnetic force does it experience?
why: Zero force for motion parallel to B follows from F = qvB sin(theta)

front: A rod of length $L$ moving at speed $v$ perpendicular to field $B$ generates motional emf $\varepsilon = {{c1::BLv}}$.
why: Motional emf BLv is prep-book detail; induction is tested qualitatively

front: A vertical wire carries current straight upward. You stand east of it. Which way does its magnetic field point at your position?
why: Right-hand rule for a wire field at a point is commonly asked

front: After a velocity selector, why does a mass spectrometer separate ions by mass?
why: Mass spectrometer separation by m/q is a common passage step

front: An electromagnetic blood flowmeter reads a transverse voltage $V = BLv$, so its signal is proportional to {{c1::flow velocity}}.
why: Blood flowmeter is a near-restatement of motional emf; passage would supply

why: Transformer turns ratio is circuits-adjacent, plausible but secondary

why: MRI vs CT radiation risk is off-outline clinical trivia

front: Contrast a motor with a generator in energy terms.
why: Motor vs generator energy conversion is supporting context

front: Faraday's law gives $\varepsilon = -N\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$, where the minus sign encodes {{c1::Lenz's law}}.
why: Faraday law with Lenz minus sign; core, but restates the Faraday card

front: Ferromagnets stay magnetized after the external field is removed because their aligned {{c1::domains}} persist.
why: Ferromagnetic domains are prep-book detail, not outline

front: For a negative charge, the magnetic force points {{c1::opposite}} to the direction given by the right-hand rule.
why: Reversing the right-hand rule for negative charges is a perennial trap

front: Give the magnetic force on a moving charge.
why: F = qvB sin(theta) is the foundational magnetic force equation

front: How do paramagnetic and diamagnetic materials differ at the electron level?
why: Para vs diamagnetic electron-level distinction is commonly tested

front: How do you determine which end of a solenoid is its north pole?
why: Solenoid north-pole rule is a secondary right-hand-rule application

front: How does Earth's magnetic field compare in strength with a clinical MRI field?
why: Earth vs MRI field strength numbers are trivia

front: How does MRI work in principle?
why: MRI principle appears often in passages; spin alignment and RF is enough

why: TMS is an off-outline application a passage would explain

front: In a cyclotron, why is the orbital period of a charged particle independent of its speed?
why: Cyclotron period independence is a secondary derivation

front: In a velocity selector, undeflected particles satisfy $qE = qvB$, so the selected speed is $v = {{c1::E/B}}$.
why: Velocity selector v = E/B is a standard calculation

front: Induced emf depends on the {{c1::rate of change}} of flux, so a loop sitting motionless in a huge steady field has no induced emf at all.
why: Emf needs changing flux, not flux; core induction concept

front: Inside a long solenoid the field is $B = {{c1::\mu_0 nI}}$, uniform and directed along the axis.
why: Solenoid B = mu0 n I is prep-book detail, rarely calculated

front: Ions accelerated through the same potential difference then bent by the same field: heavier ions follow {{c1::larger}} radii.
why: Same-voltage ions and radius vs mass is a common two-step question

front: Magnetic flux is given by:
why: Flux definition; restates the cloze flux card

front: Magnetic flux through a loop is $\Phi = {{c1::BA\cos\theta}}$, where $\theta$ is measured from the surface normal.
why: Phi = BA cos(theta) with theta from the normal is the flux definition

front: Magnetic force is maximum when velocity and field are:
why: Max force when perpendicular follows from sin(theta); common discrete

front: MRI excites protons with a radiofrequency pulse tuned to the {{c1::Larmor}} frequency, proportional to field strength.
why: Larmor frequency naming is off-outline detail

front: MRI images hydrogen in water and fat, so {{c1::cortical bone}} and air-filled lung return little signal and appear dark.
why: MRI bone and air appearance is clinical trivia

front: MRI relies primarily on:
why: Restates the MRI principle card

front: Name three ways to change the flux through a loop and induce an emf.
why: Three ways to change flux is a standard induction question

front: Power is transmitted at very high voltage because line losses scale as {{c1::$I^2R$}}.
why: I^2 R line loss belongs to circuits and is covered there

front: Protons precess at about $42.6$ MHz per tesla, so a $1.5$ T MRI uses radiofrequency near {{c1::64 MHz}}.
why: 42.6 MHz per tesla is trivia

front: State Faraday's law.
why: Faraday law is the core induction equation

front: State Lenz's law in terms of what the induced current opposes.
why: Lenz law direction reasoning is tested nearly every administration

front: State Lenz's law.
why: Restates the Lenz law card

front: The magnetic field inside a long straight wire's center is:
why: Field at the exact center of a wire is trivia

front: The strength of a wire's magnetic field varies with distance as:
why: B = mu0 I/(2 pi r) with 1/r falloff is the standard wire-field equation

front: Transformers work only with {{c1::alternating}} current, because a constant flux induces no emf.
why: Transformers need AC; supporting induction detail

front: Two isotopes of equal charge enter a mass spectrometer at the same speed. Which lands farther out?
why: Isotope separation by radius is a common mass-spec question

front: Two parallel wires carry current in opposite directions. Do they attract or repel?
why: Parallel wires attract or repel is a common discrete

front: Two parallel wires carrying current in the same direction {{c1::attract}} one another.
why: Restates the parallel-wires card

front: What do gradient coils contribute to MRI?
why: Gradient coils are off-outline MRI engineering detail

front: What field does a straight current-carrying wire produce?
why: Circular field around a wire and right-hand rule are core

front: What is the role of the strong static field in an MRI scanner?
why: Third restatement of the MRI static-field principle

front: What path does a charge take entering a uniform $B$ field perpendicular?
why: Circular path for perpendicular entry is the foundational case

front: Why are pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants, and loose steel objects hazardous near an MRI magnet?
why: MRI safety hazards are clinical trivia

front: Why do magnetic field lines form closed loops?
why: No magnetic monopoles and closed field lines is a standard discrete

front: Why does a magnet dropped down a copper pipe fall unusually slowly?
why: Eddy-current braking is a Lenz application, plausible passage context

front: Why does an MRI scanner bang loudly during a scan?
why: MRI noise mechanism is trivia

front: Why does deoxygenated blood change the MRI signal in functional imaging?
why: Deoxyhemoglobin paramagnetism links to BOLD; plausible passage step

front: Why does MRI image hydrogen nuclei rather than other nuclei?
why: Why MRI images hydrogen is MRI detail beyond the outline

front: Why does the magnetic force do no work?
why: Why magnetic force does no work; restates the no-KE-change card

why: ECG lead loops in MRI is clinical safety trivia
